lead: Chromatography and electrophoresis both separate the molecules of a mixture. Chromatography uses a moving mobile phase and a stationary phase; each solute divides between them differently and so travels at its own speed. Electrophoresis uses an electric field: a charged molecule feels a force qE and drifts at a speed set by its charge and friction. Clinical labs use these methods for glycated haemoglobin, drug levels, urine steroids, amino acids, serum proteins, haemoglobin variants and DNA. Only a few universities teach this chapter; others meet the ideas in analyser specifications.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for UV absorbance and the densitometer, and 3.7 for a clear serum before the run.

blocks.text: A mixture is placed at the start of a column or sheet. The mobile phase is a gas or liquid that flows and carries solutes. The stationary phase is a solid or liquid film that does not move. Each solute divides between the phases. A solute that spends more time in the stationary phase is retarded more and leaves later. Separation is by partition (dissolves in both phases) or adsorption (sticks to the solid).

Retention time t<sub>R</sub> is time from injection to a peak maximum. Two solutes separate when their retention times differ and peaks do not overlap too much. Thin-layer chromatography uses a coated plate and a rising solvent; paper chromatography uses water held in paper fibres; column chromatography packs the stationary phase in a tube.

Gas chromatography (GC) uses a carrier gas and a heated column; a flame ionisation detector burns organic molecules and measures ion current. HPLC uses small packed particles, so liquid is pumped at high pressure; a UV detector at 280 nm is common for proteins. Clinical uses: glycated haemoglobin, drug levels, urine steroids, amino acids.

sections.h3: Electrophoresis: speed set by charge and friction

blocks.text: An electrophoresis tank applies an electric field E (V/m) across a buffer-soaked support. A molecule with charge q (C) feels force qE. It accelerates until friction balances that force, then drifts at speed v (m/s).

blocks.where: v is drift speed (m/s); μ is mobility (m²/V·s); E is field strength (V/m); q is charge (C); f is friction factor (N per m/s).

blocks.text: The sign of the charge follows buffer pH relative to the protein's isoelectric point pI. At pH 8.6 serum proteins are net negative and migrate to the anode. Mobility depends on charge, size and shape.

Paper and cellulose acetate carry serum proteins and haemoglobin variants. Agarose gel is used for DNA, negative from phosphate groups. SDS-PAGE binds SDS, masks protein charge and makes all proteins negative, so they separate by molecular weight: smaller moves faster. Isoelectric focusing uses a pH gradient; a protein stops at its pI, where net charge is zero. Capillary electrophoresis uses a narrow tube and high voltage.

Serum protein electrophoresis on cellulose acetate at pH 8.6 gives albumin, α₁, α₂, β and γ bands. Albumin is fastest and most abundant. A densitometer scans the stained strip and reports each band as a percentage of total protein.

figure.caption: A mixture is carried by the mobile phase past a stationary phase that retards some solutes more than others; the UV detector at 280 nm records each solute as a peak against retention time.

spec.title: Separation by moving and stationary phase
spec.aria: A mixture is placed on the stationary phase, the mobile phase carries the solutes along at different speeds, and the detector records each solute as a separate peak against time.

examples.question: Serum protein electrophoresis on cellulose acetate at pH 8.6 is run on a sample with total protein 70 g/L. The densitometer reads albumin 60 %, α₁ 4 %, α₂ 9 %, β 12 % and γ 15 %. Calculate the albumin and γ-globulin concentrations in g/L.
examples.answer: Albumin is 42 g/L and γ-globulin is 10.5 g/L.
examples.check:
total = 70.0
alb_frac = 0.60
gamma_frac = 0.15
print(alb_frac * total)
print(gamma_frac * total)

traps: At pH 8.6 serum proteins are net negative and move to the anode; albumin is fastest, γ slowest.
Retention time belongs to chromatography; migration distance or mobility belongs to electrophoresis.
SDS-PAGE reports molecular weight, not net charge, because SDS masks the protein's own charge.
In HPLC the small packed particles are the stationary phase; high pressure is needed for flow, not heating.
In isoelectric focusing the protein stops at pH = pI because net charge is zero, even though the field remains on.

quiz.q: Define mobile phase and stationary phase in chromatography.
quiz.a: Mobile phase flows and carries solutes; stationary phase stays fixed and retards them.

quiz.q: Why does a solute that spends more time in the stationary phase leave later?
quiz.a: It is retarded more, so its retention time is longer.

quiz.q: List the serum protein bands at pH 8.6, fastest first.
Why does SDS-PAGE separate proteins by molecular weight, not net charge?
quiz.a: SDS masks intrinsic charge and gives similar negative charge per mass; size then controls speed.

quiz.q: Total protein is 68 g/L and albumin is 55 %. Find the albumin concentration.
A protein with pI 5.0 is placed in electrophoresis at pH 8.6. Predict its charge and direction.
quiz.a: pH is above pI, so the protein is net negative; it moves to the anode.

beyond: Not for the exam. Clinical labs increasingly couple HPLC or capillary electrophoresis to mass spectrometry for drug and metabolite measurement. Capillary electrophoresis is used for haemoglobin variant screening and some HbA1c methods. SDS-PAGE with western blotting is a research and diagnostic tool for specific proteins. Search next for HPLC, capillary electrophoresis, SDS-PAGE and isoelectric focusing.
